To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The Tormes Dome was affected by crustal melting at 320 Ma.
(1) The timing of decompression melting and anatexis of the gneisses in the Tormesian Dome is ca. 320 Ma.

(1) the Tormes dome is a gneiss-corer dome in the Central Ibarian Zone of the Iberian Variscides; (2) it was emplaced in the Carboniferous; (3) its emplacement was related to the extensional collapse phase of the Variscides; and (4) it was derived from melting of crustal rocks that had a long geological history.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the timing of the crustal melting event and the sources of the magmas.
the timing and sources of Varisican syn-kinematic granitoids in a gneiss core of the Central Iberia Zone of the Varisican orogenic belt in Spain, using U–Pb geochronology on zircon and monazite.

the timing and sources of the Variscides crustal melting and recycling, and it shows that the Variscan orogeny is a good example of how a continental collision can be followed by extensional collapse, and how this can lead to a fast recycling of the crustal materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Variscan crustal melting in the Central Ibrarian Zone is a result of the interaction of several processes: (a) crustal thickening, (b) crustal melting and (c) crustal recycling/canabilization.

the Variscan crustal melting event in the Torme Dome was triggered by extensional collapse of a crustal root, and the source for this melting event was the crustal material itself, which was already highly differentiated, as indicated by the presence of inherited zircon.
the Tormes plutonic suite is a product of the melting of the crust, with a significant contribution of recycled material, and with the involvement of mantle-derived melts in some of the plutons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Tormes granitoid pluton emplacements are related to decompression melting of the crust, triggered by collapse of the Variscides, and that the source of this crustal melting was a heterogeneous mixture of juvenile crustal materials (ca. 320 Ma) as old as Archaean.

the Tormes granitoids were emplaced in the late Carboniferous (320 Ma) as a result of crustal melting triggered by the collapse of the Variscides, and that their source was a mixture of juvenile crustal components and older crustal rocks (ca. 320 Ma and inherited zircons from the Paleozoic to the Archaean).

the Variscan crustal melting event in the Tormse Dome took place in the late Carboniferous (320 Ma) and that the source rocks were a mixture of Paleozoic (ca. 340 and ca. 390–432 Ma) and Proterozoic–Archaean (ca. 900–2700) crustal rocks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
crustal melting is a very effective way for recycling crustal material, even in a short time span of 15 My, which can be considered as the time scale at which orogens are built and destroyed.

the crustal sources of these anatectic granites were not only the Paleozoic basement of the Central Iberia Zone but also older crustal rocks, which were incorporated into the orogen during the Variscan orogeny.

the Tormes granitoid suite, as well as other similar plutons in the Central Ibero-Armorican arc, is the product of a long-lived crustal anatexis process (at least 1 Ga) that started in the Ediacaran and continued until the Late Devonian.
